newsitem.title: JAPAN: Smoke, but no fire yet, in Japan pols' Nomura ties.
newsitem.headline: Smoke, but no fire yet, in Japan pols' Nomura ties.

text.p: A payoff scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd moved closer to the political world on Tuesday with ministers' admissions of deals with the tainted firm.
But observers say the affair is unlikely to catch political fire and may end as merely a minor nuisance to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's government.

No politicians have been linked to the main scandal, which has seen the arrests of three Nomura executives suspected of making illegal payoffs and two racketeers suspected of receiving the payments from the firm, Japan's largest broker.

But a by-product of the case -- Nomura's revelations that some 9,000 elite customers, including bureaucrats and politicians, hold special "VIP accounts" -- has cast a harsh light on politicians' cozy ties with big business even though no illegal or unethical activity has been alleged yet.

Hashimoto, who was forced to begin his second term last November by apologising for a money-for-favours scandals at the health and trade ministries, has adamantly denied he or his family were among Nomura's preferred clients.
Hashimoto has even dropped hints of lawsuits against a weekly magazine which placed him and most other top ruling and opposition politicians on Nomura's VIP list.
"If my name is really there, it can only mean that someone assumed it falsely," he told reporters, chastising them for even treating gossip-prone weeklies as a news source.
Hashimoto's denial followed the revelation by the government spokesman that three of the 20 members of the cabinet currently had dealings with Nomura.
"The dealings were in government bonds and trust funds...none of which are instruments in which special favours could be granted," Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference.

Kajiyama added that investigations would continue over whether other politicians, their families, employees or political support groups had VIP accounts or special treatment from the brokerage, but questioned the need to single them out.
Stressing that he was stating a personal opinion, he said : "Do we really want to make Nomura in particular the issue?"
But political observers said the revelations were at the least embarassing to a political elite long tainted by corruption and were likely to spark a media feeding frenzy.
However, barring new developments, it would be only a "minor distraction" to Hashimoto -- not least because top opposition leaders are also rumoured to be Nomura VIPs.
"It doesn't seem likely that the politicians will beat each other up over this," said John Neuffer, political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
"It will only get ugly if a Nomura staffer steps forward with allegations, a smoking gun is found or the prosecution makes a dammning disclosure," he said.
One parliamentary source told Reuters that prosecutors have been able to move on Nomura without government interference precisely because no politicians were involved at this stage.

The source, who refused to be identified, said Nomura's payoffs made it a perfect scapegoat for the Hashimoto government as it fends off skepticism about the seriousness of its pledges to free up financial markets over five years.
"That's why Nomura became an easy target, an ideal kind of scapegoat, ahead of the Big Bang financial reforms," he said.

Nomura's ex-president Hideo Sakamaki, who has resigned over the affair, has insisted that only two former directors were involved in the payoffs. But Japan's securities watchdog agency has alleged that Nomura as a company was also to blame.
Hashimoto has personal reasons to welcome Nomura's comeuppance, observers said.

In October 1991, Hashimoto was forced to resign as Finance Minister following revelations that Nomura and three other top brokerages improperly covered elite clients for investment losses totalling nearly $1.6 billion.

That setback cost Hashimoto an early crack at the prime ministers office and kept him out of cabinet line-ups until 1994, when he took the trade portfolio in the government of his predecessor as prime minister, Tomiichi Murayama.
